en: The Peace Chant:
Oṃ. May we hear with our ears what is auspicious, O Gods; may we see with our eyes what is auspicious, O Holy Ones.
With steady limbs and bodies, may we praise you and attain that lifespan ordained by the gods.
May Indra of far-reaching fame grant us well-being; may Pūṣan, the all-knowing, grant us well-being;
may Tārkṣya, whose wheel-rims are unharmed, grant us well-being; may Bṛhaspati bestow well-being upon us.
Oṃ! Peace! Peace! Peace!
Oṃ. That is fullness; this is fullness. From fullness, fullness arises.
When fullness is taken from fullness, fullness alone remains.
Oṃ, peace! Peace! Peace!
Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad, Verse 1:
"Om"—this syllable is all this; its further explanation is as follows: that which has been...
Everything that has been and everything that will be is indeed the syllable Om;
and whatever else transcends the three periods of time, that too is indeed the syllable Om.
For all this is Brahman; this Self is Brahman. This very Self has four quarters.
Verse 3:
Having the waking state as its sphere, cognizant of external objects, having seven limbs and nineteen mouths, the consumer of gross objects, Vaiśvānara is the first quarter.
Verse 4: Abiding in the state of dream, inwardly conscious, having seven limbs and nineteen mouths, enjoying what is subtle— the Taijasa is the second quarter.
Verse 5:
That state wherein one who is asleep desires no desire whatsoever and sees no dream whatsoever is deep sleep (*suṣupta*).
In the state of deep sleep, having become one, being a mass of consciousness alone, consisting of bliss, enjoying bliss, and having the mind as its gateway— this is the third quarter, the Prājña.
Verse 6:
He is the Lord of all; He is the All-knowing; He is the Inner Controller; He is the source of all, for He is indeed the origin and the dissolution of all beings.
The all-pervading Viśva is indeed consciousness external [to the body], while Taijasa is consciousness internal [to the body].
The one who possesses dense wisdom and likewise the wise one are considered to be threefold, though they are but one.
Verse 2:
Viśva is situated in the right eye; Taijasa is within the mind; and Prājña is in the space of the heart. Thus, he is established in three ways within the body.
Verse 3:
For Viśva always experiences the gross, Taijasa the subtle, and Prājña likewise experiences bliss; understand that enjoyment is thus threefold.
Verse 4:
The gross [state] satisfies the universe; the subtle, however, satisfies the Taijasa; and bliss likewise satisfies the Prājña. Understand this threefold satisfaction.
Verse 5:
Whatever is proclaimed as the object of enjoyment and the enjoyer within the three abodes—
he who knows both of these, while enjoying, is not defiled.
Verse 6:

It is the settled conclusion that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the source of all existing things; it generates everything, as does the Person (*puruṣa*), who produces the various parts of the mind separately.
Verse 7:
Others who contemplate creation consider it to be a manifestation or an emanation;
by others, creation is conceptualized as being like a dream or an illusion.
Verse 8:
Those certain about creation hold that the Lord’s creation is mere will;
those who contemplate time believe that the birth of beings proceeds from time.
Verse 9:
Others say that creation is for the sake of enjoyment, while others say it is for the sake of sport.
This is the inherent nature of the Divine; what desire could there be for one whose every wish is already fulfilled?
Neither inwardly cognitive, nor outwardly cognitive, nor cognitive of both.
It is neither a mass of consciousness, nor consciousness, nor non-consciousness;

it is invisible, beyond conventional discourse, ungraspable, without characteristics, unthinkable, and indefinable; its essence is the realization of the one Self, it is the cessation of conceptual proliferation, and it is peaceful.
They consider the auspicious non-duality to be the fourth; that is the Self, that is to be known.
The imperishable Lord and Master is the sovereign over the cessation of all sufferings.
The Lord, who is the non-duality of all states of being, is remembered as the pervasive Fourth (turya).
Verse 11:
Viśva and Taijasa are considered to be bound by both cause and effect;
Prājña is bound by the cause alone; but these two do not exist in the Fourth (turya).
Verse 12:
The wise one perceives nothing at all—neither self nor other, neither truth nor falsehood; he is the Fourth (turya), the eternal seer of all.
Verse 13:
The non-apprehension of duality is equal for both the Prājña and the Turya states;
however, the Prājña is accompanied by the seed-sleep, whereas that [sleep] does not exist in the Turya.
Verse 14:
The first two [states] are associated with dream and sleep; the wise one, however, is associated with the absence of both dream and sleep.
Those who are certain do not perceive sleep nor indeed dream in the fourth state.
Verse 15:
For one who perceives otherwise, it is a dream; for one who does not know reality, it is sleep.
When those two errors have perished, one attains the fourth state.
When the individual soul, sleeping through beginningless illusion, awakens, it then realizes the non-dual reality— unborn, sleepless, and dreamless.
Verse 17:
If conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) existed, it would undoubtedly cease.
This duality is mere illusion; in the ultimate sense, there is non-duality (*advaita*).
Verse 18:
If the imagined were negated by anyone, then conceptual construction would cease; this discourse exists for the sake of instruction, but once [reality] is known, duality is not found.
This very Self is the imperishable syllable *oṃ*, corresponding to the long vowel (*mātrā*).
The quarters are the measures, and the measures are the quarters: namely, the letter *a*, the letter *u*, and the letter *m*.
Verse 9:

Vaiśvānara, whose sphere is the waking state, is the letter *a*, the first *mātrā*. This is because of attainment (*āpti*) or because of being the beginning (*ādimattva*); for he indeed attains all things.
And he who knows thus becomes one for whom desires have no beginning.
Verse 10:
The Taijasa, situated in the state of dream, is the letter *U*, the second *mātrā*.
Because of its excellence (*utkarṣa*) or because it stands between both, it indeed causes the continuity of knowledge to excel, and it is common to both.
There is no one in his family who is ignorant of Brahman, for he who knows thus.
The state of deep sleep is the wise one (prājña), the letter *m*, the third measure. It is so called because of measuring (*miti*) or because of merging (*apiti*).
Indeed, he who knows this measures all this, and he becomes the merger.
When there is a desire to express the "A" nature of the Viśva, the commonality of the initial [letter] is predominant.
And in the case of the non-apprehension of measure, there would be only the commonality of attainment.
Verse 20:
In the cognition of fire, an excellence is clearly observed;
likewise, when there is no apprehension of the [specific] measure, there would be a state of duality.
In verse 21:
When there is the state of the letter *ma*, for the wise man there is the predominance of mental commonality;
but when there is no perception of the measure (*mātrā*), there is indeed the commonality of dissolution.
Verse 22:
That great sage who, being firm in his conviction, knows the equality and commonality in the three abodes— he is worthy of worship by all beings and indeed to be saluted.
The letter *A* leads to the Viśva state; the letter *U* likewise leads to the Taijasa; and the letter *M* leads again to the Prājña; beyond these, no further destination exists.
The fourth is without measure, beyond empirical usage, the cessation of the phenomenal world, auspicious, and non-dual.
In this way, he who knows thus—the syllable Om—is himself the Self that enters the Self by means of the Self; he who knows thus, he who knows thus.
One should know the syllable Om part by part; the parts are the measures (mātrās), without a doubt.
Having understood the syllable Oṃ part by part, one should not think of anything at all.
Verse 25:
One should yoke the mind to the *praṇava*; the *praṇava* is the fearless Brahman.
For one who is constantly disciplined in the *praṇava*, no fear exists anywhere.
Verse 26:
Indeed, the syllable *praṇava* is the lower Brahman, and the *praṇava* is remembered as the higher.
The *praṇava* is without prior, without interior, without exterior, without posterior, and imperishable.
Verse 27:
Indeed, the *praṇava* is the beginning, the middle, and likewise the end of everything.
Having thus known the *praṇava*, one attains that immediately thereafter.
Verse 28:
One should know the Praṇava as the Lord, residing in the heart of all;
having realized that the Omkara is all-pervading, the wise man does not grieve.
He by whom the syllable *oṃ* is known— that which is measureless, infinite in measure, and the auspicious cessation of duality— is a sage, and no other person.
